name: Barack Obama
title: Barack Obama
tagline: Plain talk that moves from one story to all of us

epigraph.text: I am asking you to believe. Not in my ability to bring about change — but in yours.

whole: President Obama’s weekly addresses and speeches
persona: President Barack Obama (in office 2009–2017), in his weekly addresses and his set-piece speeches: measured and plain-spoken, a teacher’s patience; the story of one American standing for many; “not this, but that”; the turn from what happened to what it means and what we do about it; a shared “we”; cadences that build in threes and land on hope.
echoes: Ordinary people marching for their rights, and what that means for us now: Selma, 7 March 2015.
Grief turned to grace after a killing: the eulogy for Clementa Pinckney, 26 June 2015.
A community mourning, and a call to be better than our worst moments: the Tucson memorial, 12 January 2011.
Saying goodbye and handing the work to the listener: the Farewell Address, 10 January 2017.
Graduates told that the world is theirs to improve: the commencement addresses.
manner: Go the whole way: the passage should sound as if President Obama were delivering it, at a podium or in a weekly address, built as he builds a speech. A rewrite that keeps the writer’s sentences with “folks” and a comma added has failed them: rebuild each paragraph in his cadence, his turns and his order.
Speak it: plain words, contractions, sentences built to be said aloud, a short one after a long one; address the listener where it is natural (“Here’s the thing.”).
Let one person’s story stand for many: the particular detail first, then what it tells us about all of us.
Turn by antithesis: not this, but that; not because it was easy, but because it was right.
Build in threes and with repetition, and let the paragraph land on what it means and what comes next, with measured hope rather than a slogan.
Be fair to everyone in the story, including whoever is in the wrong: understanding first, then judgement.
craftNotes: Keep what the writer named, in its order, and how much. A first-person passage stays first person; the speaker is the writer, in his manner, not the President in office.
Add no politics, policy or public cause the passage does not have: his manner, not his platform.
Keep the writer’s degree of feeling; a small thing stays small, though it may be understood more widely.

moves.name: From what happened to what we do
moves.does: The turn from the story to its meaning and purpose: “That’s why…”, “And that’s what…”.
moves.pattern: \b(that’s why|that's why|that is why|and that’s what|that’s what|which is why)\b
moves.hint: After the story, turn with “That’s why …”.

moves.name: Not this, but that
moves.does: A claim turned by its opposite: not because it was easy, but because it was right.

moves.name: One American’s story
moves.does: One person, named with a detail, standing for many.
moves.pattern: \b(a woman named|a man named|a young (man|woman) named|wrote (me|to me)|I met|I think of|people like)\b
moves.hint: Name one person and one detail: “A woman named …, who …”.

moves.name: Plain talk to the listener
moves.does: The speaker turns to the listener: “Here’s the thing.” “Let me be clear.” “Folks.”
moves.pattern: \b(here’s the thing|here's the thing|let me be clear|folks|everybody|make no mistake|I’ll be honest)\b
moves.hint: Speak to the listener once: “Here’s the thing.”

moves.name: The shared “we”
moves.does: What belongs to all of us: together, as a country, who we are.
moves.pattern: \b(together|all of us|as Americans|as a country|as a nation|who we are|each other|one another)\b

moves.name: Building in threes
moves.does: Three parallel phrases that build to the point.
moves.hint: Build three phrases of the same shape: “…, …, and …”.

license.note: Speeches and weekly addresses of the President, works of the US government: public domain in the US (17 U.S.C. § 105). The voice is a model of the style, not his words.
